planting.note: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part sun to light shade in early spring; Arisaema sazensoo does not offset readily, so set out several tubers together to build a colony over time.

directions: Plant tubers in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part sun to light shade; native to Japan, Arisaema sazensoo produces a pair of five-leaflet leaves on a roughly foot-tall stem, with the flower rising separately between them on its own short stalk. The pitcher-shaped spathe narrows to a slender spadix and an unusually long, trailing spathe tip that cascades down over the front of the hood, a signature feature that distinguishes it from its many relatives. Because this species rarely produces offsets on its own, collectors typically grow a small group together rather than relying on a single tuber to multiply. All plant parts contain irritating calcium oxalate crystals and are toxic if ingested, so site it away from pets and children.

planting.note: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep in evenly moist, humus-rich soil in part sun to shade in late spring as the soil warms; Arisaema saxatile reliably produces offsets, so an established colony will slowly expand on its own.

directions: Plant tubers in evenly moist, humus-rich soil in part sun to shade; native to China, Arisaema saxatile sends up two leaves of five to seven leaflets in late spring, followed by a small white, pitcher-shaped spathe from which a dark green, tongue-like spadix appendage hangs downward for several inches. Unusually for the genus, the bloom carries a pleasant lemony fragrance rather than the carrion-like odor common among many cobra lilies. It tolerates both drier shade and damper rain-garden conditions better than many Arisaema and offsets reliably to form a spreading clump over the years. All plant parts contain irritating calcium oxalate crystals and are toxic if ingested, so keep it away from pets and children.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online (POWO)

planting.note: Plant tubers 4-5 inches deep in rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in part sun to light shade in early spring; Arisaema yamatense is one of the taller Japanese species and benefits from a sheltered site out of strong wind.

directions: Plant tubers in rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in part sun to light shade; native to Honshu, Japan, Arisaema yamatense is a tall, architectural species whose purple-and-white patterned pseudostem can top three feet, with a single leaf carried near the summit above the hooded flower. The green-and-white striped spathe encloses a contrasting white-throated interior, making the bloom conspicuous against the dark foliage. Its stately height and limited availability make it a centerpiece for a serious Arisaema collector's shaded border. All plant parts contain irritating calcium oxalate crystals and are toxic if ingested, so site it well away from pets and children.

planting.note: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep in average, humus-rich soil in part sun in mid-spring; Arisaema franchetianum breaks dormancy later than many Arisaema and may not show growth above ground until early summer in cooler zones.

directions: Plant tubers in average, humus-rich soil in part sun; native to the forests of southwestern China, Arisaema franchetianum carries large trifoliate leaves above a dramatic spathe striped in dark purple-brown and white, blooming from early to midsummer. In colder parts of its hardiness range the tuber waits until late in the season to send up growth, so mark its location to avoid disturbing it while dormant. Still uncommon in cultivation, it has been the source of at least one named selection offered by specialty nurseries, a sign of its appeal to collectors building a varied jack-in-the-pulpit collection. All plant parts contain irritating calcium oxalate crystals and are toxic if ingested, so keep it away from pets and children.
sources: Ontario Rock Garden and Hardy Plant Society

planting.note: Plant tubers about 4 inches deep in cool, moist, peaty woodland soil in full to part shade in early spring; Arisaema utile tolerates more sun than most relatives if the soil stays consistently moist and the site is not overly hot.

directions: Plant tubers in cool, moist, peaty woodland soil in full to part shade; found wild in montane forests across the Himalaya from Pakistan to Nepal and Bhutan into western China, Arisaema utile flowers from mid-spring into early summer as the purple spathe, boldly marked with white veins, unfurls alongside a long, thick spadix before the leaf fully expands. It is one of the more adaptable Himalayan species, accepting a sunnier spot than most as long as moisture is reliable, and has a long history of local medicinal use in its native range in addition to its ornamental appeal. All plant parts contain irritating calcium oxalate crystals and are toxic if ingested, so site it away from pets and children.

planting.note: Plant tubers about 5 inches deep in humusy or gravelly, well-drained soil that stays evenly moist through spring and early summer, in partial shade.

directions: Plant tubers in humusy or gravelly, well-drained soil that does not dry out in spring and early summer, in partial shade; native to the mountains of Kyushu, Japan, Arisaema maximowiczii carries a single leaf of roughly ten narrow leaflets to one side of a dark purple pseudostem. The spathe, in shades of purplish or green with a contrasting white hood, opens before the leaf has fully unfurled, giving the flower an unusually prominent early display. It remains scarce in cultivation outside specialty collections, making it a worthwhile addition for gardeners seeking lesser-known Japanese woodland aroids. All plant parts contain irritating calcium oxalate crystals and are toxic if ingested, so keep it away from pets and children.
